concept_html:
"Which features matter?" has a trustworthy answer and a misleading one.

The misleading one is impurity importance, feature_importances_ on scikit-learn tree ensembles. It is computed on training data and favours features with many distinct values. In this course's build (scikit-learn 1.9, random forest, 3,000 rows), a meaningless column of random IDs with 3,000 distinct values got an impurity importance of 0.335, half as much as the real signal (0.661).

The trustworthy one is permutation importance on held-out data: shuffle one column, breaking its link with the target, and measure how much the score drops. A feature the model relies on causes a large drop. The same random ID column dropped the test AUC by 0.004: nothing.

from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
result = permutation_importance(model, X_test, y_test, scoring="roc_auc",
                                n_repeats=10, random_state=0)
result.importances_mean, result.importances_std

Read it with three cautions:

  • It measures the model, not the world. A large drop means this model uses the feature. It does not mean the feature causes the outcome.
  • Correlated features share credit. If age and years_since_birth_cohort carry the same information, shuffling one leaves the other, and both look unimportant. Group correlated features and permute them together, or report them as a group.
  • Use the spread. Report the mean drop with its standard deviation across repeats. A drop of 0.003 ± 0.004 is zero.

Use the metric you report for the model. An importance in accuracy on imbalanced data says little (lesson B12-L1).

lines: import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.base import ClassifierMixin
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
def permutation_drop(model: ClassifierMixin, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series, col: str, rng: np.random.Generator, n_repeats: int) -> float:
"""Mean fall in held-out ROC AUC when col is shuffled."""
base = roc_auc_score(y, model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1])
drops = []
for _ in range(n_repeats):
shuffled = X.assign(**{col: rng.permutation(X[col].to_numpy())})
drops.append(base - roc_auc_score(y, model.predict_proba(shuffled)[:, 1]))
return float(np.mean(drops))

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.base import ClassifierMixin
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score


def permutation_drop(model: ClassifierMixin, X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series, col: str, rng: np.random.Generator, n_repeats: int) -> float:
    """Mean fall in ROC AUC when col is shuffled.

    Args:
        model: Fitted classifier with predict_proba.
        X: Held-out features.
        y: Held-out labels.
        col: Column to shuffle.
        rng: Seeded generator.
        n_repeats: Number of shuffles.

    Returns:
        Mean of base AUC minus shuffled AUC.
    """
    base = roc_auc_score(y, model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1])
    drops = []
    for _ in range(n_repeats):
        shuffled = X.assign(**{col: rng.permutation(X[col].to_numpy())})
        drops.append(base - roc_auc_score(y, model.predict_proba(shuffled)[:, 1]))
    return float(np.mean(drops))

title: Permutation importance on held-out data
why_html: A retention model's slide showed "customer ID" as the third most important driver, from feature_importances_. The product team asked what it meant. It meant nothing: the ID had thousands of distinct values, so trees split on it to memorise training rows. Permutation importance on the test set gave it zero. The slide had already been shown to the client.
